outline.title: Intro to 8085 Assembly – Beginner Course
outline.description: A concise introduction to the 8085 microprocessor assembly language. Students learn the fundamentals of 8085 architecture, basic instructions, and simple programs, building a solid foundation for further study.
objectives: Understand the basic architecture and components of the 8085 microprocessor.
Learn and apply fundamental 8085 assembly instructions and addressing modes.
Write, assemble, and debug simple 8085 assembly programs.
Develop skills to analyze and troubleshoot basic assembly code.
Prepare for more advanced microprocessor programming topics.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 – 8085 Architecture & Basic Assembly Concepts
learning_objectives: Identify key hardware components of the 8085 microprocessor.
Describe the role of registers, flags, and memory in 8085 operation.
Explain the purpose of the assembler and its output.
Understand instruction format and addressing modes.
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces the 8085 microprocessor’s architecture, covering the CPU, memory, I/O, and control signals. Students learn the basic structure of assembly language, the function of the assembler, and how instructions are formatted. The session concludes with a hands‑on exercise to write a simple "Hello, World!" program in 8085 assembly.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 – Fundamental Instructions & Data Movement
learning_objectives: Execute data transfer instructions such as MOV, MVI, LXI, LHLD.
Use immediate, register, and memory addressing modes.
Load, store, and move data between registers and memory locations.
Understand the use of the accumulator in arithmetic operations.
lessons.summary: Building on the foundation, this lesson covers data movement instructions, emphasizing how to transfer data between registers, memory, and the accumulator. Practical examples demonstrate the use of immediate and register addressing. Students practice assembling code that loads values into registers, stores them to memory, and manipulates data using the accumulator.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 – Arithmetic, Logic, Control Flow & Debugging
learning_objectives: Perform arithmetic operations (ADD, SUB, INR, DCR).
Implement control flow with JUMP, CALL, RET, and conditional branches.
Employ debugging techniques using breakpoints and register inspection.
lessons.summary: The final lesson introduces arithmetic and logical instructions, control flow mechanisms, and debugging strategies. Students write a small calculator program that adds two numbers, then use conditional jumps to display results. The module ends with a debugging walkthrough, teaching how to identify and fix common errors in 8085 assembly code.

1.title: Lesson 1 – 8085 Architecture & Basic Assembly Concepts
1.introduction: The 8085 microprocessor is the backbone of many early computer systems. In this lesson you will discover its internal structure, the role of its registers and flags, how it accesses memory, and the basics of writing and assembling code. By the end you should be able to describe the hardware layout and explain how simple instructions are formed and executed.

sections.heading: Hardware Overview
sections.explanation: The 8085 consists of a central processing unit (CPU) that contains the arithmetic logic unit (ALU), registers, flag register, and control logic, all connected to a memory bus and I/O bus. Key components include the accumulator, general‑purpose registers (B, C, D, E, H, L), the stack pointer (SP) and program counter (PC).

sections.heading: Registers and Flags
sections.explanation: Registers hold intermediate data; the accumulator (A) is used for most arithmetic. The flag register contains Zero, Sign, Parity, Auxiliary Carry, and Carry flags, updated automatically by the ALU after operations.
sections.example:
ADD C        ; Adds register C to A and sets flags accordingly
JC 0100h     ; Jump if Carry flag set

sections.heading: Assembler Role
sections.explanation: An assembler converts human readable assembly into object code (.obj) or executable (.exe). It resolves labels, calculates addresses, and produces a binary that the microprocessor can load into memory.
sections.example: LABEL:   MOV A, #05h  ; assembler turns #05h into 0x05 opcode bytes

1.summary: You now understand the 8085’s hardware core, how registers and flags work, the structure of machine instructions, and the assembler’s function in bridging human code and machine execution. These fundamentals enable you to write and assemble simple 8085 programs.

exercises.task: Write a program that loads the value 0x3A into the accumulator and stores it in memory address 0x2000 using the 8085 assembly language.
exercises.hint: Use the MOV instruction for register transfer and the STA opcode for storing the accumulator into an absolute address.

exercises.task: Explain which flag(s) will be set after executing the instruction SUB H where H contains the value 0x02 and the accumulator contains 0x01.
exercises.hint: Consider the result of the subtraction and how the zero, sign, and carry flags are affected.

questions.question: Which component of the 8085 CPU is primarily responsible for performing arithmetic operations?
questions.explanation: The accumulator (A) is the register used by the ALU for most arithmetic and logic operations.

questions.question: What does the 8085 flag register NOT contain?
questions.explanation: The flag register holds Zero, Sign, Parity, Auxiliary Carry, and Carry flags; it does not contain an Interrupt Enable flag.

questions.question: In an 8085 assembly instruction like "MOV A, B", what is being performed?
questions.explanation: MOV transfers data from source register B to destination register A.

questions.question: Which bus does the 8085 use to access general‑purpose memory addresses from 0000h to FFFFh?
questions.explanation: The 8085’s 16‑bit address bus allows access to 64K memory locations 0000h‑FFFFh.

questions.question: When the instruction "SUB H" is executed with H=0x02 and A=0x01, which flag will be set?
questions.explanation: Subtracting a larger value (0x02) from a smaller one (0x01) sets the Carry flag to indicate a borrow; Zero, Sign, and Parity are cleared.
